title: Graph Anomaly Detection with Few Labels: A Data-Centric Approach

problem.claim: Few-label anomalous node detection in static graphs is hindered by rare anomalies, costly labeling, severe class imbalance, and intricate graph learning.

gap.claim: Existing research largely treats labeled-data shortage as given, while node-generation methods and the effectiveness of synthetic data for graph anomaly detection remain unexplored.

contributions.claim: A diffusion-based graph generation method synthesizes training nodes that conform to the original graph's topology and attribute distribution and can integrate with existing anomaly detectors.
The work establishes two principles for designing denoising neural networks tailored to graph anomaly generation, based on observed shifts in graph energy distribution during diffusion.
Generated training data can enhance the performance of existing graph anomaly detectors.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on eight widely used datasets report that the generated data effectively improves the performance of nine state-of-the-art graph detectors.

narrative_sequence.summary: Static-graph anomaly detection with few labels faces rarity, labeling-cost, imbalance, and graph-learning challenges.
Prior work often treats labeled-data shortage as fixed, and synthetic-node generation for this setting remains unexplored.
The work investigates denoising diffusion and derives graph-energy observations and design principles for anomaly generation.
It proposes diffusion-based synthesis of training nodes for integration with existing anomaly detectors.
Results across eight datasets report improved performance for nine graph detectors.

source_observation.claim: Synthetic training nodes are generated to match the original graph's topology and attribute distribution.

interpretation.claim: When labels are scarce, data augmentation may be more effective when it preserves domain-relevant structural and feature distributions.

application.claim: For other structured-data detection tasks, consider augmentation methods that preserve the structure and attribute statistics used by downstream detectors.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this principle transfers beyond graph anomaly detection or across different graph distributions.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the nine detectors, eight datasets, baselines, metrics, or numerical performance changes.
The abstract does not describe the diffusion architecture, node-generation procedure, or the two design principles in operational detail.
The abstract does not report computational costs, sensitivity analyses, failure cases, or label budgets.
